The single biggest fact to internalize: when 하나 sits directly in front of a counter (개, 명, 시, 살, 마리), it loses its last syllable and becomes 한 — 한 개, 한 명, 한 시 — while the full 하나 only stands alone (as in counting "하나, 둘" or taking a particle, 하나만). nuance: 십 is the Sino-Korean number "ten," from the hanja 十 (a vertical and horizontal cross). It is the engine of the Sino tens and the whole large-number system: dates, money, minutes, floors, phone numbers, and counts beyond what native can comfortably reach. So ten o'clock is 열 시 but ten minutes is 십 분; the tens stack as 십일(11), 십이(12), 이십(20), 삼십(30). The must-know irregularity is the month: 'October' is not 십월 but 시월 — the ㅂ drops (mirroring 육월→유월 for June). English speakers regularly write 십월 and must memorize 시월. The other usual slip is using 십 for the hour (십 시 instead of 열 시). Keep dates, money, and minutes on the Sino side, 십, but remember the 시월 exception.

nuance: 만 is the Sino-Korean number "ten thousand," from the hanja 萬. The deep point for English speakers: Korean does NOT group large numbers by thousands the way English does — it groups by 만 (10,000). So 100,000 is 십만 (ten 만), 1,000,000 is 백만 (hundred 만), and 10,000,000 is 천만 (thousand 만). This 만-based grouping is the single hardest mental switch in Korean numbers, because you must constantly divide by ten-thousands rather than thousands. Unlike 백 and 천, the bill 만 원 is commonly said 일만 원 too, especially when writing checks or being precise. The classic mistake is calculating 'a million' as 천천 (thousand-thousand) — it does not exist; a million is 백만. Master the ladder 만 → 십만 → 백만 → 천만 → 억(100,000,000).
